data.rationale: FND-054 states the whole core insight. ACQ-TH1 arrives at 06:30 ICT, which is 07:30 SGT. Matching takes 45 minutes and reports another 15, so reports publish at about 08:30 SGT. That misses NFR-8's 08:00 SGT deadline, and it gets worse as volume roughly doubles by 2027. It cites 16.2 and 2.2 under NFR-8. The other hinted findings overlap the flaw's location but describe different defects. FND-022 covers missing state-machine transitions, FND-049 covers RPO and replication, and the rest are about data residency, PCI rules and network tokens.

FND-049 is the clear match for F03, and it covers all three credit items. It quotes NFR-4's requirement of zero RPO even when a whole region is lost (c1). It quotes 20.2's asynchronous Aurora Global Database replication with lag under one second (c2). It then says authorizations acknowledged in that lag window are missing from the promoted database, so the requirement and the design contradict each other (c3).

FND-048 is a weaker second candidate. It cites 20.2 and NFR-4, but its defect is different: a single HSM and no disaster-recovery copy of the Vault, which is a recovery-time problem rather than the asynchronous-replication data-loss problem.

I excluded the other findings in the location hint because each one describes a different defect.

FND-046 is the only finding that describes this defect. It says the Fraud Hook detokenises the PAN using the Card Adapter's service role and sends it to FRV-1 (13.1). It points out that this contradicts P2, the 12.1 detokenise restriction and the 12.2 scope table. It concludes that the Fraud Hook and related paths fall into CDE scope, so NFR-5 cannot be assessed as declared. It also flags the shared role as a P9 violation and notes that PAN goes to the third party. The other findings in the location hint cover different issues: FND-055 is the fail-open distractor, FND-001 is about idempotency keys, FND-017 is about phasing, FND-052 is about payout accounts and FND-043 is about data residency.

FND-034 quotes Section 9.3's claim of 10,000 WCU per partition and says it is far above DynamoDB's documented limit. It names the hot key: the merchant_id partition carrying M-0001's 900 TPS, 45% of peak. It says the write math ignores the 4 KB response body and the LSI's extra writes, and that the LSI may hit an item-collection size limit. It never states the 1,000 WCU figure, so the scoring step should check whether that meets the first credit item. The other findings are about different defects: FND-001 is the Redis key scope and FND-027 is missing concurrency tests.

FND-032 is the only finding that describes this defect. It cites Section 12.4, NFR-6 and Section 24. It says PCI DSS doesn't allow card verification codes to be kept after authorization, even encrypted. It also says that retention until settlement, or for up to 72 hours, for incremental authorizations goes past authorization by design. None of the other findings deal with sensitive authentication data or CVC retention.

FND-043 is the closest match to F07. It says NFR-7 covers only privacy law, that primary data sits in Singapore with Jakarta used only for DR, and that payment regulators may not allow offshore processing, with Indonesia, the largest market, at greatest risk. It also says this must be confirmed because the answer could change the hosting design. FND-057 is weaker. It cites NFR-7 and Section 19.1 data placement and raises transfer questions per market, but it frames them around personal-data privacy and retention. That is close to the distractor note, so it is at most a secondary candidate. None of the other findings deal with data residency.

FND-052 states the whole core insight at the flaw's location (18.3, 18.4, FR-13). MFA is enforced only for Owners. A Finance user can change the payout bank account with no step-up authentication, second approver or cooling-off period. Only the person who made the change is notified, so a phished password can redirect payouts. It also cites the P9 conflict. The two other findings named in the location hint are about different defects: FND-026 is about network-token readiness and FND-032 is about CVC retention. FND-030 concerns where customer refunds are paid and how that bank account is collected and checked, which is a different defect. No other finding covers merchant account takeover.

FND-018 is the clear match. It cites Section 21.1 and NFR-2 and says the claim that "fewer than 1% cascade" contradicts the 3.8% retryable rate in Section 10.5 (c1). It notes that a timeout-triggered cascade costs at least 2,500 ms plus a second round trip (c2). It concludes that the p99 would exceed 1,500 ms and that NFR-2's acceptance test would fail (c3). FND-047 is only a weak secondary candidate: it covers cascading after timeouts in Sections 11.1 and 11.2, but its defect is duplicate authorizations, not latency. No other finding deals with the p99 latency budget.

FND-001 states the full core insight. It says the Redis key idem:resp:{idempotency_key} has no merchant_id, which contradicts P3 and FR-5. It also says the fast path is checked before DynamoDB, and that cross-merchant collisions are likely because merchants use their own order IDs. Finally, it says the second merchant gets the first merchant's payment object and no payment is created for it. FND-027 only mentions that the acceptance test never exercises "the Redis fast path across merchants". That is the same topic, but it does not state the defect itself, so it is a weak secondary candidate. The other findings are about different defects.

FND-048 is the only finding that states this defect. It says the KEKs sit on a single HSM in ap-southeast-1a and that Section 12.1 does not cache DEKs, so every detokenise needs the HSM. Losing that HSM or its AZ therefore stops all card acceptance (about 55% of attempts). It also says this undercuts the three-AZ posture and NFR-3, and it challenges the confirmed 'one HSM at launch' decision. It cites 12.3 and NFR-3. It does not mention AWS's guidance of at least two HSMs or that the 1,500 TPS trigger is never reached, though it quotes the trigger. FND-046 (Fraud Hook detokenise), FND-026 (network tokens) and FND-032 (CVC retention) overlap the flaw's sections but describe unrelated defects.

FND-047 states the full core insight. A timeout or 5xx means the first acquirer may already have approved, and cascading then produces duplicate holds. Late approvals are discarded and never reversed. It also refutes the attempt_id claim and notes the 20.3 sweeper doesn't cover superseded attempts. Its locations (11.1, 11.2, FR-7) overlap the flaw's. FND-018 is about latency, not duplicate charges. FND-048 is about the HSM being a single point of failure, with Vault 503s cascading as a side effect.

FND-029 is the only finding about this defect. It cites FR-8, 10.3 and 26.1 and says the 2% tolerance has no unit (percentage points or relative). It also says it is unclear whether a per-transaction comparison or the weekly realised-rate review enforces FR-8, and that the acceptance test cannot settle which reading applies. The other findings in the location hint cover unrelated defects: refunds, the state machine, tokens, CVC, go-live sequencing and idempotency tests.

FND-027 says FR-5 requires correct handling of concurrent duplicates, while the acceptance test only resends after the first response. That means the test never exercises the lock or the 409 path, which is the flaw's core insight, and the finding cites 26.1 and FR-5. No other finding is about how the FR-5 acceptance test handles concurrency.

FND-026 states the core insight directly. Section 24 confirms network tokens from launch, Section 27 rates the Vault 'Ready' and Section 28 marks Phase 3 'No - ready'. Backlog item 2, however, says the TRID registration and token-service-provider agreement have not been submitted. FND-026 concludes that the readiness and phase tables overstate what is settled. No other finding covers network tokens.

The locations 26.1, 2.1 and 9.2 for FR-5 overlap the key flaw's sections, and the anchor quote is identical. The extra point about the sweeper missing IN_PROGRESS locks does not detract from the match.

The finding states the whole core insight. On the single HSM: "The KEKs sit on one HSM in ap-southeast-1a". On no caching: "Section 12.1 does not cache DEKs, so every tokenise and detokenise needs the HSM: losing that HSM or that AZ stops all card acceptance (about 55% of attempts)". On the conflict: it "undercuts the three-AZ posture in 20.1 and NFR-3" and challenges "one HSM at launch". It does not say the 1,500 TPS trigger is never reached or cite the AWS two-HSM guidance, but the credit rule is substance-based and the NFR-3 conflict is explicit, so c3 counts as stated in substance. The location (12.3, NFR-3, with 12.1 and 20.1 referenced) overlaps the flaw's location. The extra retry and DR-region points don't take away from the match.

Section 27 rates the Vault Ready, and Section 28 marks Phase 3 ... 'No - ready'" (c1). This is a match, and the finding states the core insight as a whole. On c1, it quotes FR-5's requirement of at most one provider call "including when duplicate requests arrive concurrently". The premise checks out against the document. Section 28 says "The first merchant cohort (Singapore, cards and PayNow) goes live after Phase 7". The Fraud Hook (FRV-1) is Phase 8. Phase 9 covers load, chaos and DR game days, the PCI DSS assessment and the Section 26 test plan. So real card payments would start before FR-9 fraud scoring exists, before the NFR-5 Level 1 assessment, and before any Section 26 acceptance criteria have been run. Section 27's overall conclusion names only the Admin API schemas and the dispute module as gaps that do not block the first cohort, and leaves this out. This sequencing problem is specific and grounded in the document. It does not appear among the key flaws F01–F14 or observation O01. No other finding in the review covers it: FND-026 deals with network-token readiness and FND-055 with fraud fallback behaviour, not phase ordering.

I checked the finding's premises against the document, and they hold. In §7.2, REQUIRES_ACTION can move only to AUTHORISING or CANCELLED (expiry). §8 sends wallet and bank flows to REQUIRES_ACTION, and §11.4 says a failure there "returns FAILED", which has no direct permitted path. A failed 3DS challenge has the same gap. PARTIALLY_REFUNDED can move only to REFUNDED, and REFUNDED has no outgoing transitions. So a payment refunded before settlement can never reach SETTLED, even though §16.2 moves every matched payment to SETTLED. FR-2 forbids any transition not listed, so these are real internal contradictions tied to this document. The key's flaws and its observation O01 don't cover state-machine gaps, and no other finding in the review raises this issue.

The finding cites §13.2 correctly, but it criticises a choice the document justifies. Principle P8 says optional enrichment, explicitly including fraud signals, degrades to documented defaults. §3 says principles win over later sections when they conflict, so the claimed clash with FR-9 is settled by the document's own rule. The fallback is documented and tiered (HIGH-tier merchants get REVIEW), is listed in §20.4, and is tested by the FR-9 timeout acceptance criterion. Asking for a risk owner, exposure cap or alert is generic advice. No key flaw or observation covers this, and it does not repeat another finding.

The premise is accurate. The NFR-7 validation (a DPO sign-off) sits in Phase 9. No section gives a per-market transfer basis or explains how the immutable audit records fit with retention limits, which is a real gap tied to this document. It overlaps only partly with FND-043, which is about payment-regulator rules on offshore processing and treats NFR-7's privacy-law coverage as given. It also differs from F07, which is about residency and localisation. One weaker point: the 'no field-level retention mapping' claim is partly answered by the NFR-7 acceptance criterion, which requires every personal data field to be mapped to a purpose and retention period. That mapping is only a late check, though, so the core issue still stands.

The premise is accurate. FR-15 says refunds go out "as a bank payout to the customer's nominated account" when a method has no refund API. Section 6 defines a "Payout account" only as the merchant's "Bank account for merchant payouts". The Section 19 schema has no field for a customer's refund destination. Section 16.3 covers only merchant payouts. The FR-15 acceptance test in 26.1 checks only that "payout-based refunds produce a payout instruction." The document never says how the customer's account is collected, validated or protected, which is a real gap in a money-moving flow. It is tied to this document rather than being generic advice. No key flaw or observation covers it (O01 concerns the Stripe/IETF attribution). No other finding in the review raises it either: FND-052 is about the merchant's payout account, and FND-057 is about cross-border data transfer in general.

data.doc_passage: card_number Vault detokenise Cross-merchant velocity graph ... FRV-1's consortium velocity graph is keyed on the full card number ... The Fraud Hook obtains the PAN through the Vault's detokenise operation, using the Card Adapter client library and service role.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 13.1 has the Fraud Hook get the full PAN through the Vault's detokenise operation, using the Card Adapter's client library and service role, and send it to FRV-1. This conflicts with Section 12.1, which says only the Card Adapter may detokenise, and with the Section 12.2 table, which places the Fraud Hook out of scope as handling only the token, BIN and last 4.
data.rationale:
The document contains every passage the finding relies on:
- **Section 13.1:** the request payload includes card_number, obtained through Vault detokenise. The Fraud Hook gets the PAN using the Card Adapter's client library and service role.
- **Section 12.1:** "Only the Card Adapter's service identity may call detokenise."
- **Section 12.2:** lists "Fraud Hook Out of scope Token, BIN, last 4 only."
- **P2:** says PAN never leaves the Vault boundary except over the Card Adapter's connection to an acquirer.
- **Section 5:** exposes detokenise-for-adapter through a private endpoint to the core VPC.
- **Backlog item 4:** the FRV-1 data processing agreement is still pending.

So the contradiction the finding describes is really in the document.

data.doc_passage: The CVC is required for the initial customer-initiated authorization and, at several acquirers, for each re-presentation of the credential during a cascade and for incremental authorizations (ride-hailing tips, hotel extensions). The Vault therefore stores the CVC encrypted under a separate KEK, and deletes it when the Reconciliation Service marks the associated payment SETTLED, or after 72 hours, whichever is first. This is permitted by PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2, which allow sensitive authentication data to be retained in encrypted form until the transaction is settled.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document has the Vault store the CVC in encrypted form until settlement or for up to 72 hours. It justifies this by saying PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 allow sensitive authentication data to be kept in encrypted form until the transaction settles. It also cites incremental authorizations as one reason the CVC is needed after the first authorization.
data.rationale: Section 12.4 matches what the finding says: the CVC is kept encrypted until settlement, with a 72-hour maximum. The document cites PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 as allowing this and lists incremental authorizations as a reason. NFR-6 and the 'CVC handling' entry in Section 24 repeat the same position. Whether that reading of PCI DSS is correct is the finding's conclusion, and this check does not judge it.

data.doc_passage: On completion of a request, the final response is written to idem:resp:{idempotency_key} with a 24-hour TTL. On every incoming mutating request, the Payments API checks this key first; on a hit, it returns the stored response immediately without touching DynamoDB or the Orchestrator.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 9.2 caches final responses in Redis under idem:resp:{idempotency_key}, a key that includes neither merchant_id nor the request hash, and returns the cached response on a hit without checking DynamoDB. This conflicts with P3's (merchant, key) scoping and FR-5's 422-on-different-body rule, and Section 9.1 says merchant order or invoice IDs are accepted as keys.
data.rationale: Section 9.2 builds the Redis key from idempotency_key alone, with no merchant_id and no request hash. On a hit, the stored response goes straight back without the hash comparison done on the DynamoDB path. Confirmed Decisions repeats the key as "idem:resp:{key}". P3 scopes idempotency to (merchant, key). FR-5 requires a 422 when a key is reused with a different body. Section 9.1 says merchants often use their own order or invoice identifiers as keys and that this is accepted. Every part of the finding's premise matches the document.

data.doc_passage: Recovery point objective for authorized payments and ledger postings shall be zero, including on loss of an entire AWS region. ... Aurora Global Database replicates the payments and ledger cluster to ap-southeast-3. Replication is storagelevel and asynchronous, with typical lag under one second. • MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache are not replicated cross-region; on regional failover they are recreated empty in ap-southeast-3 from infrastructure-as-code, and in-flight idempotency state is reconstructed from the payment table.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: NFR-4 requires zero RPO on region loss, yet Section 20.2 depends on asynchronous Aurora Global Database replication with sub-second lag and says idempotency state is rebuilt from a payment table (Section 19) that holds no idempotency key or request hash; a 30-minute failover is also longer than NFR-3's monthly downtime budget.
data.rationale: The document backs every part of this finding. NFR-4 requires zero RPO, including when a whole region is lost. Section 20.2 says cross-region replication is asynchronous with typical lag under one second, and that idempotency state is reconstructed from the payment table. The payment table DDL in Section 19 has no idempotency_key or request_hash column, only merchant_reference. Those two fields live only in the DynamoDB table, which is recreated empty on failover. The downtime figure also checks out: NFR-3 sets 99.95% availability, which allows about 21.6 minutes of downtime per 30-day month, and the failover target is 30 minutes. All three quoted passages appear in the document.

data.doc_passage:
8 Fraud Hook (FRV-1) Yes - vendor contract (Backlog item 4)
9 Hardening - load, chaos and DR game days; PCI DSS assessment; Section 26 test plan Follows Section 26
The first merchant cohort (Singapore, cards and PayNow) goes live after Phase 7; other markets follow at four-week intervals.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 28 schedules first-cohort go-live after Phase 7, but places the Fraud Hook in Phase 8 and the PCI DSS assessment, load/chaos/DR game days and the Section 26 test plan in Phase 9, both after go-live.
data.rationale: The Section 28 phase table matches the finding. Phase 8 is the Fraud Hook (FRV-1). Phase 9 covers hardening: load, chaos and DR game days, the PCI DSS assessment and the Section 26 test plan. The text then says the first cohort goes live after Phase 7. Section 26 also calls its table "the basis for the test plan in Build Phase 9." FR-9 requires fraud scoring of every card payment before authorization. So the order the finding describes is what the document says.

data.doc_passage: On a retryable outcome, the Retry Engine immediately submits a new attempt, with a new attempt_id, to the next acquirer in the Routing Engine's candidate list. ... Because each attempt carries its own attempt_id and the previous attempt did not succeed, cascading cannot create a duplicate charge: the ledger records only the approved attempt. Responses that arrive for an attempt after its 2,500 ms timeout are logged against the attempt and discarded.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Sections 11.1 and 11.2 cascade immediately on a 2,500 ms timeout, HTTP 5xx or connection refused. They discard any response that arrives after the timeout, yet still claim that cascading cannot create a duplicate charge because the ledger records only the approved attempt. The 20.3 sweeper handles only payments stuck in AUTHORISING.
data.rationale: The finding's claims about the document are accurate. Section 11.1 lists "acquirer HTTP 5xx; connection refused; no response within 2,500 ms" as Retryable, with the action "Cascade to next candidate". Section 11.2 says the Retry Engine resubmits "immediately", says late responses are "logged against the attempt and discarded", and makes the "cannot create a duplicate charge" claim. Section 20.3 describes the sweeper as finding "payments in AUTHORISING for more than 30 seconds". Nothing in the document describes reversing approvals that arrive late on attempts that were superseded.

data.doc_passage: The Vault's KEKs are held in an AWS CloudHSM cluster with one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. CloudHSM takes automatic daily backups of the cluster to S3, from which a new HSM can be created in any AZ. A second HSM will be added to the cluster when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS. If the HSM is unreachable, the Vault returns HTTP 503 and the Card Adapter maps this to a retryable outcome.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document puts the Vault's KEKs on a single CloudHSM in ap-southeast-1a with DEKs not cached, maps an unreachable HSM to an HTTP 503 that becomes a retryable (cascading) outcome, and its cross-region DR section never covers the CDE, the Vault or the HSM in ap-southeast-3.
data.rationale: The document backs each factual claim in the finding. Section 12.3 says there is one HSM in ap-southeast-1a, recovery is from daily backups, and an unreachable HSM produces a 503 that the Card Adapter treats as retryable. Section 12.1 says "DEKs are not cached", so each detokenise call needs the HSM. Section 24 confirms "one HSM at launch". Section 11.1 lists HTTP 5xx as a retryable outcome that triggers cascading. Section 20.2 covers only Aurora Global Database, and MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache being rebuilt from scratch in the DR region. Nowhere does the document describe a Vault, CDE or HSM in ap-southeast-3; Section 5 places the CDE cluster in the primary region only. The 55% card share comes from the volume table.

data.doc_passage: Cascading does not move the p99 because fewer than 1% of card payments cascade; the cascade path therefore sits above the 99th percentile.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 21.1 leaves cascades out of the p99 latency budget on the grounds that fewer than 1% of card payments cascade, but the document also states that 3.8% of card attempts are retryable, that retryable outcomes (including a 2,500 ms timeout) trigger a cascade, and that the NFR-2 acceptance test injects 3.8% retryable outcomes.
data.rationale:
I checked each quote against the document and they are all accurate:
- Section 21.1 uses the "fewer than 1%" figure to leave cascades out of the budget.
- Section 10.5 says retryable outcomes are 3.8% of card attempts.
- Section 11.1 lists "no response within 2,500 ms" as a retryable trigger, with the action "Cascade to next candidate".
- The Section 26.2 acceptance test for NFR-2 runs with "3.8% retryable-outcome injection".
- NFR-2 says the 1,500 ms p99 limit includes "any cascade".

Since every retryable card outcome is cascaded, the document's own numbers put cascades at about 3.8% of card payments, not under 1%. The premise is supported.

data.doc_passage: A Finance or Owner user can change the payout bank account in the portal. The change takes effect from the next payout cycle. A confirmation email is sent to the user who made the change, and the change is written to the audit log.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The finding says Section 18.4 lets one Finance or Owner user change the payout bank account, notifying only that user. It says the document specifies no step-up authentication, second approver, cooling-off period or verification gate, even though the payout account has a verified_at field. It also says MFA is enforced only for Owners, the Finance role can both issue refunds and edit the payout account, and the back-office console requires a second approver.
data.rationale: Section 18.4 matches the finding: one Finance or Owner user can make the change, and the confirmation email goes only to that user. Nowhere else does the document add step-up authentication, a second approver, a cooling-off period or a verification gate for this change. The payout account entity in Section 6 does include a verified_at field. Section 18.3 enforces TOTP only for the Owner role and leaves it optional for everyone else. Section 18.2 gives the Finance role both "Issue refunds" and "edit payout bank account". Section 18.5 requires the back-office console's write actions to have approval from a second staff member. Every factual part of the premise holds.

data.doc_passage: The batch matcher starts once all expected files for business day T have been received, so that cross-provider netting and multi-provider payouts are computed on a complete day. ... At 2025 volume, the matcher's measured end-to-end run time is 45 minutes, and merchant settlement report generation takes a further 15 minutes.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document has the batch matcher wait until every expected settlement file for day T has arrived. ACQ-TH1's file lands at 06:30 ICT (07:30 SGT), and matching takes 45 minutes plus 15 minutes for reports at 2025 volume, so reports would be ready around 08:30 SGT, after the NFR-8 deadline of 08:00 SGT.
data.rationale: Section 16.2 says the matcher waits until all files have arrived. Section 16.1 lists ACQ-TH1's delivery time as 06:30 ICT. ICT is UTC+7 and SGT is UTC+8, so that is 07:30 SGT. Matching takes 45 minutes and reports take 15 more, so publication lands around 08:30 SGT. NFR-8 requires reports by 08:00 SGT on T+1, so the deadline is missed. Section 16.2 also says matched payments become SETTLED, and Section 16.3 computes payouts after settlement. Unmatched lines go to the Finance Operations queue, and the document gives no capacity or service level for handling them.

data.doc_passage: REQUIRES_ACTION -> AUTHORISING | CANCELLED (expiry) ... CAPTURED -> SETTLED | PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED ... SETTLED -> PARTIALLY_REFUNDED | REFUNDED / PARTIALLY_REFUNDED -> REFUNDED
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 7.2's permitted transitions omit transitions that other sections rely on: REQUIRES_ACTION cannot go to FAILED, even though Section 11.4 says wallet and bank failures return FAILED, and a payment that is PARTIALLY_REFUNDED or REFUNDED cannot move to SETTLED, even though Section 16.2 moves matched payments to SETTLED.
data.rationale: The finding's claims match the document. Section 7.2 allows REQUIRES_ACTION to move only to AUTHORISING or CANCELLED, and PARTIALLY_REFUNDED to move only to REFUNDED. Neither refund state can move to SETTLED. Section 11.4 says a failed wallet or bank payment "returns FAILED". Section 8 says that after a wallet or bank payment enters REQUIRES_ACTION, the provider's notification "drives the final transition". Section 16.2 says "Matched payments transition to SETTLED". FR-2 allows only the transitions listed in Section 7. The FR-2 test in Section 26 checks only that no transition falls outside Section 7.2. Neither section says how holding a capture after REVIEW, or making several partial captures, appears as a state.

data.doc_passage: DynamoDB serves each partition key value from a single partition, and a single partition sustains up to 10,000 write capacity units per second. Our largest merchant (marketplace M-0001) peaks at approximately 900 create-payment TPS during campaign events (45% of 2,000 TPS). Each request consumes two writes - lock acquisition and completion update - or about 1,800 WCU at peak, comfortably within the perpartition ceiling.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: Section 9.3 claims that a single DynamoDB partition sustains up to 10,000 WCU per second. It sizes M-0001's idempotency writes as two writes per request, about 1,800 WCU at 900 TPS, without counting item size or LSI writes, and keys the table by merchant_id with an LSI on created_at. Section 9.1 says that a request arriving after the 24-hour retention period is treated as new.
data.rationale: Section 9.3 contains the 10,000 WCU per-partition figure and the 1,800 WCU calculation word for word, and it counts one WCU per write. It doesn't account for the 4 KB response_body item size (the size appears only in the 9.2 table), and it doesn't count the extra LSI writes. The table uses merchant_id as the partition key and has an LSI on created_at (9.2 and 9.3). Section 9.1 says "A request after expiry is treated as new," and 9.2 relies on a conditional put with attribute_not_exists and a ttl attribute. So the document says what the finding claims. Whether 10,000 WCU is the real DynamoDB limit is a separate question from what the document states.

data.doc_passage: Send a create-payment request; after its response is received, resend the identical request with the same Idempotency-Key. The second response is byte-identical to the first and the acquirer simulator records exactly one authorization. Resending with a modified body returns 422.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: FR-5 requires the identical response and at most one provider call even when duplicate requests arrive concurrently, but its Section 26.1 acceptance test only resends the request after the first response has arrived, so it never tests concurrent duplicates, the 409 in-flight path, cross-merchant fast-path behaviour or crash recovery.
data.rationale: FR-5 does say "including when duplicate requests arrive concurrently". The FR-5 acceptance test in Section 26.1 resends only after the first response has come back. It tests only the byte-identical replay and the 422 on a changed body. It does not test concurrent duplicates, the 409 request_in_progress path, keys reused by different merchants, or a crashed pod's lock. The sweeper in Section 20.3 is described as finding payments in AUTHORISING, and that section says only that it "also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS". So the document does match the finding's description.

data.doc_passage: Hard timeout 150 ms. On timeout or vendor error: LOW and MEDIUM risk-tier merchants receive ACCEPT; HIGH risk-tier merchants receive REVIEW.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: When FRV-1 times out or errors, the design accepts payments for LOW and MEDIUM risk-tier merchants without a score, and names no risk owner, exposure cap or alert for that unscored volume. Meanwhile P8 treats fraud signals as optional, FR-9 requires every card payment to be scored, and the vendor SLA is still pending.
data.rationale: Section 13.2 says that on a timeout or vendor error, LOW and MEDIUM merchants get ACCEPT. P8 lists "fraud signals" as optional enrichment that falls back to documented defaults. FR-9 says every card payment shall be scored before authorization. Backlog item 4 confirms the FRV-1 SLA is not yet agreed. I searched Sections 13, 20.4 ("Fraud vendor down: Default decisions per risk tier") and 22, and the Confirmed Decisions table, for any cap, alert, metric or named owner covering fallback-accepted volume and found none. The risk team is named only as the owner of the score-to-decision thresholds, not of the fallback exposure.

data.doc_passage: 2. Token Requestor onboarding - Visa VTS and Mastercard MDES token-requestor registration (TRID) and the commercial agreement with a token service provider; certification test plan. Application not yet submitted.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The document makes network tokens the primary card-on-file credential from launch and marks the Vault and Phase 3 (card-on-file with network tokens) ready. Backlog item 2, however, says the VTS/MDES token-requestor application has not been submitted, and the readiness and phase tables do not reflect this.
data.rationale: The document backs every part of the premise. Section 24 says "Network tokens (VTS/MDES) as the primary credential for all card-on-file and recurring payments from launch". Section 27 rates the Card Vault and Card Adapter "Ready", citing network tokens as specified. Section 28 lists Phase 3 as "card-on-file with network tokens" and marks it "No - ready". Backlog item 2 says "Application not yet submitted". Neither the readiness table nor the phase table mentions Backlog item 2.

data.doc_passage: NFR-7 Privacy review DPO sign-off per market; every personal data field is mapped to a purpose and retention period.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The design keeps personal data from five markets in ap-southeast-1, replicates it to ap-southeast-3, and sends device, IP and hashed identity data to FRV-1 while the DPA is pending. Audit before/after records are kept immutable for five years. Yet the design gives no per-market transfer basis, no field-level retention mapping and no way to square immutable audit payloads with NFR-7 retention limits. Its only check is a DPO sign-off in the Phase 9 validation.
data.rationale:
The document backs each factual point in the finding:
- Section 19.1 puts all primary stores in ap-southeast-1, with an Aurora Global DB secondary in ap-southeast-3.
- Section 13.1 sends device fingerprint, IP address, user agent and SHA-256 email/phone to FRV-1.
- Backlog item 4 lists the FRV-1 data processing agreement as still pending.
- Section 22 and NFR-12 keep audit records with before/after values under Object Lock for five years.

I searched for anything on cross-border transfer basis or transfer mechanisms and found nothing. Retention in Section 19.1 is set per record type (payment records 7 years, webhooks 30 days, and so on), not per personal-data field. The "no personal data" statement covers only the ledger (Section 14.3), not the audit records. The field-level purpose and retention mapping appears only as an acceptance criterion for NFR-7 (DPO sign-off), and that test plan runs in Build Phase 9.

data.doc_passage: All primary data stores (Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, MSK, S3 intake and archive buckets) are in ap-southeast-1. The Aurora Global Database secondary in ap-southeast-3 (Jakarta) is used for disaster recovery only (Section 20).
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: The design puts all workloads and primary data in Singapore, with DR in Jakarta. Its only regulatory data requirement (NFR-7) covers personal data protection laws. It never addresses whether payment-system or financial-sector regulators in the five markets allow offshore processing and storage. It also never addresses the cross-border implications of replicating every market's data to Jakarta for DR.
data.rationale: Section 5 says all workloads run in ap-southeast-1 (Singapore). Section 19.1 places the primary data stores there and the DR secondary in Jakarta. NFR-7 lists only personal data protection laws (SG PDPA, MY PDPA, ID Law 27/2022, TH PDPA, PH DPA). I searched for data residency, localisation, onshore or offshore processing, payment-system or central-bank regulators (MAS, BI, BNM, BOT, BSP), and cross-border data transfer for DR. None of these appear anywhere in the document. The 4,200 Indonesia merchants and the QRIS/bank-transfer flows are as the finding states. The only regulatory items the design addresses are PCI DSS and personal data, so the absence claim holds.

data.doc_passage: Refunds shall be supported for every payment method; where a method has no refund API, the refund shall be executed as a bank payout to the customer's nominated account. ... FR-15 Refund test per method: Full and partial refunds succeed per method; payout-based refunds produce a payout instruction.
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: FR-15 says refunds for methods with no refund API go by bank payout to the customer's nominated account. The document never says how that account is collected, validated, stored or protected. The only payout account it models is the merchant's (Section 6), Section 19 has no field for it, and the FR-15 test only checks that a payout instruction is produced.
data.rationale: The document mentions the customer's nominated account only once, in FR-15. Nothing else covers it. Section 6 defines the payout account as "Bank account for merchant payouts." Section 16.3 Payouts covers only merchant payable balances. The Section 19 tables have no customer bank-account field. NFR-7 is generic and doesn't address this data. The FR-15 acceptance criterion only checks that a payout instruction is produced. I found no synonym (beneficiary, customer bank details, refund destination) that fills the gap.

data.doc_passage: FR-8: "For each transaction, the Routing Engine shall prefer the lowest-cost eligible acquirer unless doing so reduces the expected authorization rate by more than 2%." §10.3: "At routing time, the engine compares the approval prior of the lowest-cost acquirer against that of the highest-approval acquirer and applies the cost preference when the difference is within the configured tolerance (default 2). Separately, the weekly Routing Review compares each merchant's realised authorization rate under cost-preferred routing against a control slice (5% of traffic routed approval-first)..." §26.1 FR-8: "For a set of synthetic transactions with configured costs and approval priors, the selected acquirer matches the expected choice."
data.label: SUPPORTED
data.premise: FR-8 states a "more than 2%" authorization-rate tolerance and Section 10.3 states "tolerance (default 2)" without saying whether this means percentage points or a relative change. Section 10.2's weighted score, 10.3's cheapest-vs-highest-approval comparison and the weekly control-slice review are all described as routing mechanisms. The FR-8 acceptance test only checks that the "expected choice" is selected.
data.rationale: The finding quotes FR-8, §10.3 and §26.1 accurately. §10.3 gives "default 2" with no unit. Neither that section, FR-8, nor §24 ("cost-preferred within 2 tolerance") says whether the 2 is percentage points or a relative change. §10.2 does define a weighted score that includes w_cost. §10.3 does describe both a per-transaction comparison and a weekly review against a control slice. The FR-8 test only checks for an "expected choice" and does not define the threshold.

items.rationale: The passage says Section 9.2 writes final responses to idem:resp:{idempotency_key}. It also says a hit returns the stored response immediately without touching DynamoDB, so the key holds only the client key. This is the part of the claim it is cited for.
The passage states P3: idempotency is scoped to the pair of merchant identity and client key. That is the principle the claim says the Redis key contradicts.

Section 9.1 says merchants frequently use their own order or invoice identifiers as keys, and that this is accepted. It also states the 422 rule for a reused key with a different body. Both points are cited in the claim.

The passages show a key with no merchant scope, merchants using order or invoice IDs, and the 422 body-mismatch rule, so cross-merchant collisions and skipping the 422 are well supported. However, 'sequential' order IDs is an unstated assumption. The 'FR-5' label does not appear in the source passages. The inference also does not establish the claimed outcomes of no payment being created or goods shipped without payment, though the bypass of the Orchestrator suggests the first.
The passage directly says that on a hit, the stored response under idem:resp:{idempotency_key} is returned without touching DynamoDB or the Orchestrator.

The passages support a merchant-agnostic key, merchants using order IDs, payment suppression through the Orchestrator bypass, and the stale response replacing the HTTP 422. The figure of 15,000 merchants and the assumption of sequential IDs do not appear in any cited passage, so the inference's 'likely in normal use' rests partly on unstated facts.

Backlog item 4 shows the FRV-1 data processing agreement and SLA are not yet finalised. This supports the claim that PAN goes to a third party whose DPA is still pending.

The passages do show a mismatch: an out-of-scope Fraud Hook receives PAN, and detokenise is exposed to the core VPC. But none of the derived passages includes NFR-5 or its Report on Compliance test. Directly states that the Fraud Hook obtains the PAN through detokenise, using the Card Adapter client library and service role.

Section 12.4 says the Vault stores the CVC encrypted under a separate KEK. It deletes it at SETTLED or after 72 hours, whichever comes first, and cites PCI DSS v4.0 3.2.1/3.3.2 as allowing this. That establishes both the design and its stated basis.
The passage states the basis the claim cites: PCI DSS v4.0 Requirements 3.2.1 and 3.3.2 'allow sensitive authentication data to be retained in encrypted form until the transaction is settled.'

The passage says the CVC is required for incremental authorizations (ride-hailing tips, hotel extensions) as well as the initial authorization. That establishes the incremental-authorization use case the claim cites.

The passages list the initial authorization and the later incremental authorizations as separate uses, and keep the CVC until settlement or for up to 72 hours. So the design keeps the CVC after the initial authorization by intent. The document only asserts the PCI permission and never checks it. This matches the claim's 'by construction' point.
The confirmed decisions table lists 'CVC handling: Encrypted in Vault until settlement, max 72 hours', which establishes the confirmed CVC decision named in the claim.
The passage directly states the retention rule: delete at SETTLED or after 72 hours, whichever comes first. This matches the claim's 'until settlement or for up to 72 hours'.

EV-086 supports the links the claim depends on. NFR-5 requires a PCI DSS v4.0 Level 1 assessment, and NFR-6 relies on 3.2.1/3.3.2 with deletion at settlement. The document asserts the PCI permission without checking it. However, the inference also says the 72-hour limit makes later incremental authorizations impossible, and none of the passages establish that.

The passages show the CVC is kept for cascades and incremental authorizations. But the derived passages say nothing about cascade timing, so the premise that cascades finish in about 7.5 s is not established. The conclusion about incremental authorizations agrees with the claim, but part of the reasoning rests on facts not given here.

The passage says the RPO for authorized payments and ledger postings must be zero, including on loss of an entire AWS region. The NFR labels in the extracted text are jumbled, but EV-070 confirms this is NFR-4.

The passage says Aurora Global Database replication of the payments and ledger cluster is storage-level and asynchronous, with typical lag under one second. This matches the claim's description of 20.2.

The passage says that on regional failover the DynamoDB, MSK and ElastiCache stores are recreated empty, and in-flight idempotency state is reconstructed from the payment table. This is the 20.2 statement the claim quotes. It does not show the Section 19 schema, but that is not what this item is cited for.
The passage says regional failover has a target duration of 30 minutes, which is the figure the claim uses.

EV-008 and EV-068 establish that asynchronous replication with non-zero lag cannot guarantee zero RPO, and the 2,000-payment estimate follows from lag at 2,000 TPS. However, the key point that the Section 19 payment table has no idempotency_key column is not in any of the source passages, so the FR-5 conclusion is unsupported here.

The arithmetic is roughly right: about 21.6 minutes for a 30-day month, or 21.9 minutes for an average month. But the only source passage (EV-158) gives the 30-minute target, not the 99.95% figure. The inference also assumes the whole failover counts as API downtime.

The NFR-4 DR game day requires every ledger posting committed before the failure to be present after failover, which supports the zero-RPO requirement for ledger postings. It does not cover authorizations, the replication mode, or the idempotency and availability points.
The passage says monthly availability of the merchant payment API must be at least 99.95%. This is the NFR-3 budget behind the claim's figure of about 22 minutes.

EV-008 (the zero-RPO requirement) and EV-068 (asynchronous replication with sub-second lag) establish that an unplanned regional loss can drop the last lag window of commits. So RPO is not zero, which supports the claim's RPO conflict.
The passage says outright that the first cohort (Singapore, cards and PayNow) goes live after Phase 7. That is the part of the claim this item is cited for.
The phase table lists Phase 8 as the Fraud Hook (FRV-1), which is what this item is cited to show.
The table lists Phase 9 as hardening: load, chaos and DR game days, the PCI DSS assessment and the Section 26 test plan. That matches the claim.
FR-9 says every card payment must be scored by the fraud-scoring hook before authorization. That establishes the FR-9 requirement the claim relies on.

The source passages show go-live after Phase 7, the fraud hook in Phase 8, the PCI assessment and Section 26 test plan in Phase 9, and the FR-9 scoring requirement. So the point that FR-9 is unmet at launch is supported, provided the phases run in sequence. None of the passages defines NFR-5 or says Section 26 is the release or acceptance gate, so those parts are not established.

The source passages show the phase ordering and the go-live point. But no passage gives FR-9's content or NFR-5's definition, so the requirement-violation parts of the inference rest on assumptions the passages don't state.

The source passages show go-live happens before the Phase 8 Fraud Hook and that FR-9 requires card payments to be scored before authorization, so 'unscored, contrary to FR-9' is supported. No passage includes the Section 27 readiness conclusion, so the contradiction with Section 27 is not established.

The passage says responses arriving after the 2,500 ms timeout are logged and discarded, and that the ledger records only the approved attempt. It does not list the triggers (5xx or timeout), show that two holds can result, or mention the 20.3 sweeper.

The passage shows the cascade is immediate, the 'cannot create a duplicate charge' assertion, that the ledger records only the approved attempt, and that late responses are discarded. The point that the assertion fails for ambiguous outcomes is the reviewer's reasoning, not something the passage states. The sweeper is not covered.

The passage lists HTTP 5xx, connection refused and no response within 2,500 ms as retryable outcomes that cascade, and says the Retry Engine resubmits immediately. That covers the trigger part of the claim but not the double-hold consequence or the sweeper.

The cited passages show an immediate cascade on timeout or 5xx, late responses being discarded, and a ledger that records only the approved attempt. The document itself expects late responses to arrive, so a late approval from the first acquirer would stay live and unrecorded. That establishes the double-hold part of the claim this item is cited for. It does not address the sweeper.

FR-5 states the requirement of at most one authorisation per idempotency key. It says nothing about cascade triggers, discarded late responses, double holds or the sweeper, so it does not establish any part of the claim.

The inference that a timeout is an unknown outcome, so a discarded late approval leaves a live authorisation, is well grounded in the passages. However, it covers only the timeout case, not 5xx, and does not establish that the hold is never reversed or anything about the sweeper.

The cascade/discard passages and FR-5 support the core inference that a discarded late approval leaves a second live authorisation that conflicts with FR-5. P1 is not in the passages, the 'no void' point is assumed rather than shown, and it covers only timeouts, not 5xx or the sweeper.

The passage shows that Section 21.1 leaves cascades out of the p99 because 'fewer than 1% of card payments cascade', and that it sums to 1,338 ms against the 1,500 ms target. That is the part of the claim this item is cited for.
The passage states that retryable outcomes are 3.8% of card attempts and that cascading recovered about 31% of them. Both figures match the claim.

The passage defines 'no response within 2,500 ms' as a retryable outcome that cascades to the next acquirer with a new attempt. So a timeout-triggered cascade takes at least 2,500 ms plus another attempt, which is over 1,500 ms.
The passage quotes NFR-2: p99 end-to-end card authorization 'including any cascade' shall not exceed 1,500 ms.
The passage shows that the NFR-2 acceptance test runs under NFR-1 load with 3.8% retryable-outcome injection and requires p99 ≤ 1,500 ms.

The sources establish that about 3.8% of attempts are retryable and cascade, which is above 1%. That contradicts the reason Section 21.1 gives for leaving cascades out. They also show that timeout cascades exceed 1,500 ms. However, the passages do not say what share of the 3.8% are timeouts rather than fast soft declines or 5xx errors. A soft decline followed by a quick second attempt could finish under 1,500 ms. So 'the slowest 1% are mostly cascaded' and 'likely to fail' depend on an unstated assumption that timeouts, or slow cascades in general, make up more than about 1% of payments in the test mix.

The passage says the KEKs are held in a CloudHSM cluster with one HSM in ap-southeast-1a. It also says a replacement HSM is created from automatic daily backups, which matches the 'rebuilt from the daily backup' part of the claim.

The passage says DEKs are not cached and each detokenise call unwraps the DEK inside the HSM. Because the KEKs that wrap the DEKs are held in CloudHSM, the passage shows that card operations depend on the HSM.

The passage says that if the HSM is unreachable, the Vault returns HTTP 503 and the Card Adapter maps this to a retryable outcome. That is the part of the claim it is cited for. The 'up to three times' cascade figure does not appear here.
Section 20.1 says every service runs at least three replicas across three AZs. This establishes the three-AZ posture that a single-AZ HSM would undercut.

Section 20.2 lists Aurora replication, plus MSK, DynamoDB and ElastiCache being recreated, and does not mention the Vault, the CDE or the HSM. However, the passage is cut off partway through. A missing mention in a truncated excerpt does not prove 20.2 leaves them out, and the passage does not establish the 30-minute failover conclusion.

The derived passages establish one HSM, the 1,500 TPS trigger for a second HSM, the per-call DEK unwrap and the HMAC key held in the HSM. The 55% card share and the 2,000 TPS peak do not appear in the cited derived passages. 'Several thousand operations per second' is an estimate the passages do not support. Load capacity is also only indirectly relevant to the claim.
The passage says a second HSM is added only when sustained card volume exceeds 1,500 TPS. This confirms the 'one HSM at launch' decision that the claim challenges.
The volume table gives the card share of attempts as 55% in the 2027 design target. This supports the 'about 55% of attempts' figure.
The passage directly states that the Vault returns HTTP 503 when the HSM is unreachable and the Card Adapter maps this to a retryable outcome.
The passage contains NFR-3 (at least 99.95% monthly availability) and the NFR-4 recovery time objective of 30 minutes. These are the targets the claim cites.

The calculation 1,100 card TPS < 1,500 TPS, meaning one HSM through 2027, is established by EV-081 and EV-083. Read with the 503 behaviour, EV-024 supports the point that HSM loss fails card authorisations. However, NFR-3 is not among the derived passages, and the restore duration is never given. So a conflict with 99.95% availability depends on unstated assumptions.
The passage says the batch matcher starts only once all expected files for business day T have been received. That establishes the gating premise.

The passage states that at 2025 volume the matcher takes 45 minutes and report generation a further 15 minutes. It also confirms that matching drives the SETTLED transition and sends exceptions to Finance Operations.
The intake table lists ACQ-TH1 as delivering daily at 06:30 ICT. That is the latest delivery in the table.
Payment attempts go from 5.1 M per day in 2025 to a 10.5 M target in 2027. That supports the claim that volume roughly doubles.

The timing arithmetic (07:30 SGT plus 60 minutes gives about 08:30 SGT) follows from the sources. The exception estimate does not. It assumes settlement lines equal payment attempts and uses the 2027 figure of about 10 M. It also treats the 99.9% target as the actual rate. None of the passages show that no capacity or service level is defined for Finance Operations.
The passage directly states that the batch matcher starts once all expected files for business day T have been received.
NFR-8 requires at least 99.9% auto-match and requires merchant settlement reports to be published by 08:00 SGT on T+1. This establishes the target the claim says is missed.

The arithmetic is correct: 06:30 ICT is 07:30 SGT, and adding 45 and 15 minutes gives 08:30 SGT. But the 08:00 SGT NFR-8 target is not in any of its source passages (EV-014, EV-016, EV-131), so the 'missed' conclusion relies on a target those passages don't contain.
Section 18.4 says outright that a Finance or Owner user can change the payout bank account in the portal.

Section 18.4 lists the only follow-up steps after a change: a confirmation email to the user who made it, plus an audit log entry. It names no other recipient and no approval or verification step. Section 18.5 also confirms that back-office write actions need a second staff member's approval.
The passage says TOTP is enforced only for the Owner role at first login. That establishes that MFA is not mandatory for Finance.
The roles table gives Finance both 'Issue refunds' and 'edit payout bank account'. That establishes that one role holds both rights.

The sources support the core point: Finance can change the payout account, MFA is optional for non-Owners, the change takes effect next cycle, and the only email goes to the user who made the change. But 'T+1' appears in none of the source passages. Also, the email goes to the compromised account's own address, which may be the real user's inbox, so saying the notice goes to the attacker goes beyond the text.
'Other roles may enable it in their profile' shows MFA is optional, not enforced, for Finance and other non-Owner roles.

The passage states P9: money-moving permissions must be kept separate from configuration permissions. But it does not show that Finance holds both refund and payout account rights. It also does not classify payout account editing as a configuration permission, so the claimed P9 violation rests on an unstated assumption.

The sources do establish that Finance holds both rights (EV-085), that MFA is optional (EV-034), and that notice goes only to the actor with no approval step (EV-032). But P9's text is not among the inference's sources, so 'contradicts P9' is not established here. 'Unnoticed' also overstates things, because changes are audit-logged and an email goes to the account holder.

The Section 7.2 table shows REQUIRES_ACTION can only go to AUTHORISING or CANCELLED (expiry). It also shows that neither PARTIALLY_REFUNDED nor REFUNDED has a transition to SETTLED, which is the transition-table part of the claim.
The full 7.2 table shows PARTIALLY_REFUNDED can only go to REFUNDED, and REFUNDED has no outgoing transitions. So a payment refunded before settlement cannot reach SETTLED, as the claim says.

Section 11.4 confirms that a failed wallet or bank payment returns FAILED. It does not say the payment is in REQUIRES_ACTION when it fails. The failure could come from AUTHORISING, and AUTHORISING -> FAILED is allowed. The claim relies on an unstated assumption.

The passage states that matched payments move to SETTLED and that unmatched or mismatched lines become reconciliation exceptions. This is what the claim attributes to Section 16.2. NFR-8 is not covered here, but this item is not cited for it.

The passage shows the REVIEW outcome can be 'authorize-and-hold-capture' depending on merchant config, so the flow the claim refers to exists. The claim that it has no state representation depends on the 7.2 table, not this passage.

The cited passages support the refunded-before-settlement gap. Other parts are not established. Nothing shows wallet or bank payments fail from REQUIRES_ACTION, and AUTHORISING -> FAILED exists. The 3DS step only says 'resume on challenge result' and never mentions failure. Authorize-and-hold-capture could map to the AUTHORISED state. No passage mentions multiple partial captures, the FR-2 property test, or NFR-8.

The passage quotes Section 9.3 saying that one partition sustains up to 10,000 WCU per second. That is the doc premise this item is cited for. It does not show that the figure is wrong, but it is not cited for that.
The table definition lists response_body as a 'Serialised response, up to 4 KB', which establishes the item-size point the claim relies on.

The table definition names created_at as the 'LSI sort key lsi_created_at', so the table does have an LSI as the claim says. The passage does not itself quantify the LSI's write cost or its item-collection limit.

The 10.5 M daily-attempts figure does not appear in any passage it is derived from (EV-028/030/128). It applies the 45% peak share to daily volume and treats the 4 KB maximum as the typical item size. The claim that each write costs several WCU rests on outside metering rules. The inference itself marks the limits as unverified.
The passage directly states the two writes per request, about 1,800 WCU at peak for M-0001 at 900 TPS, and 'comfortably within the per-partition ceiling', which is the premise the claim challenges.
The volume table gives the largest single merchant's share at peak as 45% (2027 target), which supports 'the merchant carrying 45% of peak traffic'.

The 5,400 WCU figure depends on per-KB write metering, which the passages do not establish (the inference itself says 'to be verified'). It also assumes items are at the 4 KB maximum. The 20 GB estimate applies the 45% peak share to average daily volume. The source facts are present, but the conclusions need unstated assumptions.

The passages confirm that the 1,800 WCU figure counts one unit per write and gives no source for the 10,000 WCU ceiling. They also show the NFR-1 load test at 2,000 TPS and NFR-3 availability. However, 'assumes small items and no index write cost' relies on outside WCU and LSI metering knowledge. The NFR-1 test is never described as uniform, so the point about the load test is inferred. The item also does not address the TTL part of the claim.
The acceptance test resends only after the first response has arrived. So it is sequential and doesn't exercise concurrent duplicates, which is the part of the claim this item is cited for.
FR-5 states that it allows at most one downstream call and the identical response, 'including when duplicate requests arrive concurrently', exactly as the claim quotes.

This passage describes the conditional put, the 409 response for IN_PROGRESS, and sweeper recovery of crashed-pod locks. That gives the mechanisms the claim names. But it states that recovery works, and doesn't establish the gap for a lock taken before any payment row exists.

It confirms the sweeper scans payments in AUTHORISING. It also says the sweeper 'also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS', which suggests orphaned locks may be handled directly. So it doesn't clearly establish the claimed gap.

The first half holds: a sequential replay can't show concurrent deduplication. The second half assumes the sweeper only starts from payments, which EV-094's 'also completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS' leaves uncertain. None of the sources shows the sequential test skips the Redis fast path or the conditional put. The first request does perform the put.

'payment_id … Set once known' shows an IN_PROGRESS record can exist before a payment ID does, and the 24-hour TTL is documented. That supports the precondition for the claimed orphan, but not that the sweeper fails to resolve it.

The TTL and the AUTHORISING-based scan are supported. But the conclusion that such locks stay IN_PROGRESS until the TTL depends on the sweeper only finding work through payments. The cited sweeper passage also says it completes idempotency records left IN_PROGRESS, so this is an unstated assumption.

The passage states a 150 ms hard timeout, and on timeout or vendor error LOW and MEDIUM risk-tier merchants get ACCEPT, so those payments go through without a score. That establishes the fallback behaviour this item is cited for. It says nothing about the vendor SLA, Backlog 4 or the share of volume, but those parts are not what it is cited for.
FR-9 says every card payment shall be scored by the fraud-scoring hook before authorization. That directly establishes the requirement the claim attributes to FR-9.
P8 says to 'degrade gracefully on enrichment' and names fraud signals as optional enrichment that falls back to documented defaults. That matches the claim's description of P8.

The source passages show the ACCEPT fallback, the FR-9 requirement and the P8 principle. However, short excerpts cannot show that the whole document has no exposure cap, risk owner or alert. The 2,000 TPS figure and the 'most card volume' share also appear nowhere in the passages. The inference about unbounded, unowned exposure is plausible, but it depends on unstated assumptions.

Backlog item 2 lists VTS/MDES token-requestor registration (TRID), the commercial agreement with a token service provider and a certification test plan, and says 'Application not yet submitted.' That establishes the open-item part of the claim.

The decision table says network tokens (VTS/MDES) are the primary credential for all card-on-file and recurring payments from launch, with PAN only as a fallback. That matches what the claim says about Section 24.
The Section 28 build-phase table lists Phase 3 (Transaction core ... card-on-file with network tokens) as 'No - ready' for dependency on open design items. That matches the claim.
The readiness table rates Card Vault and Card Adapter as 'Ready' and says network tokens are specified. That supports the claim that Section 27 rates the Vault Ready.

The source passages do show a 'from launch' decision and a phase marked ready that both depend on a backlog item whose application has not been submitted. However, FR-14 is named in none of them, so the specific claim that the tables overstate FR-14 is not established. The 'unknown lead time' point is not stated either.

EV-035 confirms the 'from launch' decision and EV-037 gives the 'Ready' rating. EV-036 shows the token-requestor application has not been submitted and certification is still at the test-plan stage. Together they establish that both rest on work that has not started, which supports the claim's central point.

The passage says all workloads run on EKS in ap-southeast-1 (Singapore), which supports the Singapore hosting part. It does not mention primary data stores explicitly, DR in Jakarta, Indonesia's merchant count, QRIS flows, or regulators' positions on offshore processing.

NFR-7 lists only personal data protection laws for the five markets (SG PDPA, MY PDPA, ID Law 27/2022, TH PDPA, PH DPA). It does not mention payment-system or financial-sector rules, so the passage establishes the NFR-7 part of the claim.

The two source passages show Singapore hosting and an NFR-7 limited to data protection. However, two excerpts cannot establish that no requirement, decision or backlog item anywhere covers payment-regulator data-location rules. The inference also does not cover the Jakarta DR, Indonesia's 4,200 merchants, QRIS/bank-transfer flows, or the cross-border implications of DR replication.

NFR-7 names the five markets and their laws. It requires processing to follow each one, including retention limits. That covers the part of the claim this item is cited for: the five markets and the retention limits NFR-7 requires.

Section 19.1 says all primary data stores are in ap-southeast-1, with an Aurora Global Database secondary in ap-southeast-3 for disaster recovery. That supports 'stored only in ap-southeast-1 and replicated to ap-southeast-3'.
The FRV-1 request payload lists device fingerprint, IP address, and SHA-256-hashed customer email and phone. That establishes what data FRV-1 receives.
The open-items list includes 'FRV-1 contract - data processing agreement and SLA finalisation', so the DPA is still pending.

The source passages show that personal data from the five markets is stored in Singapore and sent to FRV-1, whose DPA is not finalised. But none of them mention a DPO sign-off in Phase 9 or say that the only NFR-7 check comes after build. So the inference's point about timing, which is the key part, is not backed by its sources.
The passage states FR-15 directly: when a method has no refund API, the refund is executed as a bank payout to the customer's nominated account. That is the part of the claim it is cited for.

The FR-15 acceptance criterion only requires that refunds succeed and that payout-based refunds produce a payout instruction. Nothing in it checks the destination account, which supports the claim that a wrong destination would go undetected.

The Payout account entity is described as 'Bank account for merchant payouts', with an encrypted account number and verified_at. It covers merchant accounts only and says nothing about customer refund accounts. The passage runs straight into Section 7, which places it at the end of Section 6.

The derived passages confirm that FR-15 needs a customer-nominated account, that the test checks only for a payout instruction, and that the payout account entity is for merchants only. However, the claim that 'no section defines' capture, verification or storage is about the whole document, and three excerpts cannot show that. They also say nothing about Section 19 or NFR-7.

Section 10.3 states the tolerance as 'default 2' with no unit. It describes the pairwise comparison between the lowest-cost and highest-approval acquirers, and a separate weekly Routing Review against a 5% control slice. This covers the 10.3 and weekly-review parts of the claim.
The FR-8 text applies 'for each transaction' and says 'more than 2%' without saying whether that means percentage points or a relative change. This is what the claim says about FR-8.

The passage shows a weighted score that ranks acquirers 'highest score first', with per-merchant weights. It sits just before the 10.3 heading, which supports the claim that Section 10.2 ranks acquirers by a weighted score that differs from the pairwise rule.
The FR-8 acceptance test only checks that the selected acquirer 'matches the expected choice'. It does not define a unit or say which mechanism applies, which is what the claim says.

The cited passages support the inference that the 'expected choice' is not uniquely defined, because both a weighted score and a pairwise rule apply. The 88% approval rate in the worked example does not appear in any cited passage, so that illustration is an unstated assumption. The 0.24 arithmetic is correct.
FR-8 says 'more than 2%' with no unit stated, as the claim says.

The decision table backs up the unitless 'within 2 tolerance' and the weighted cost/approval/latency score. However, it is a summary table, not Section 10.3, and it does not mention the pairwise rule, the weekly review or the test.
